name: Eat the rainbow / skin nutrient diet

card.summary: Eating many colours of produce for antioxidants in hope of better skin; antioxidant supplements have shown no benefit or small harms in trials, and no skin studies of the colour approach were found.
card.note: Food-based advice differs from high-dose antioxidant supplements, which have raised safety concerns in some trials.

quick.overview:
Eat the rainbow is the idea of eating fruit and vegetables of varied colours, which contain different pigments and antioxidants, to support health and skin. It is discussed in skin communities as a nutrient-focused approach.

Wikipedia's antioxidant article notes fruits and vegetables are good sources of vitamins C and E and carotenoids, but does not discuss skin, and reports that antioxidant supplements in trials showed no effect or a small mortality increase in vulnerable groups.
quick.mechanism: The proposal is that antioxidants and pigments such as carotenoids counter oxidative stress in the skin. Wikipedia notes that laboratory-only antioxidant measures such as ORAC are no longer considered relevant to human diets.
quick.risks: Whole produce is generally not the concern; high-dose supplements are. The CARET trial found higher lung cancer rates in smokers taking beta-carotene and vitamin A.

lead: Eating the rainbow refers to eating produce in a variety of colours for the range of nutrients and pigments they contain. Wikipedia describes fruits and vegetables as good sources of vitamins C and E and of carotenoids, noting cooking can destroy some vitamins while raising the availability of some carotenoids [1].

In skin-focused communities the approach is discussed as a way to improve complexion through antioxidants. Wikipedia's antioxidant article does not address skin, and reports that trials of antioxidant supplements found no effect or a small increase in mortality in elderly or vulnerable groups [1].
No studies of colour-variety diets for skin appearance were found in the sources reviewed.
infobox: Vitamins C and E, carotenoids, polyphenols

paras: No studies found on eating the rainbow for skin outcomes. Related research on antioxidant supplements: the CARET trial found higher lung cancer rates in smokers taking beta-carotene and vitamin A, and a meta-analysis of about 230,000 patients linked some antioxidant supplements to higher mortality in high-quality trials; these studies did not examine skin and involved supplements rather than food [1].

Wikipedia notes the USDA withdrew its antioxidant food measurements in 2012, stating they were not biologically relevant to human health, and that the ORAC method is no longer considered relevant to human diets [1].

lore.intro: Colourful produce is discussed as a skin-supporting habit.

claims.believers: Proponents say the pigments and vitamins in varied produce protect skin from oxidative damage.
claims.experts: No skin studies were found; antioxidant supplement trials have shown no benefit or small harms in some groups [1].
